Let $W$ be a subspace of a finite-dimensional inner product space $V$. For every $v\in V$, the vector $P_Wv$ is the unique point of $W$ nearest to $v$: for every $w\in W$,

$$\lVert v-P_Wv\rVert\le\lVert v-w\rVert,$$

with equality if and only if $w=P_Wv$.

Let $W$ be a subspace of a finite-dimensional inner product space $V$. The orthogonal-decomposition theorem ([[thm-finite-dimensional-orthogonal-decomposition]]) gives

$$V=W\oplus W^\perp$$

and associates to every $v\in V$ unique vectors $w\in W$ and $z\in W^\perp$ with $v=w+z$. The **orthogonal projection onto $W$** is the function

$$P_W:V\longrightarrow W,\qquad P_Wv=w.$$

Equivalently, $P_Wv$ is the unique vector of $W$ such that $v-P_Wv\in W^\perp$.

derivations.claim: Set $V:=\operatorname{span}(M\cup\{f\})$. Since $M$ is finite-dimensional and adjoining one vector increases dimension by at most one, $V$ is a finite-dimensional real inner-product space with the inherited inner product; $M$ is a subspace of $V$ and $f\in V$. Apply [F1] inside $V$ and set $p:=P_Mf$.
By [F2], $p\in M$ and $f-p\in M^\perp$.

Since $p\in M$ and $f-p\in M^\perp$, Pythagoras [F3] gives $\|f\|^2=\|p\|^2+\|f-p\|^2\ge\|p\|^2$, so $\|p\|\le\|f\|$. If $q\in M$ also has $f-q\in M^\perp$, then for every $r\in M$, [F3] gives $\|f-r\|^2=\|f-q\|^2+\|q-r\|^2\ge\|f-q\|^2$. Thus $q$ is a nearest point to $f$, and [F1] forces $q=p$.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

A **real kernel** on a set $X$ is a function $k:X\times X\to\mathbb R$. It is **positive semidefinite** if it is symmetric and, for every integer $n\ge1$, every $x_1,\ldots,x_n\in X$, and every $c_1,\ldots,c_n\in\mathbb R$,

$$\sum_{i=1}^n\sum_{j=1}^n c_i c_j k(x_i,x_j)\ge0.$$

A **real reproducing kernel Hilbert space with kernel $k$** is a real Hilbert space $\mathcal H$ of functions $X\to\mathbb R$ such that, for each $x\in X$, the section $k_x:=k(\cdot,x)$ lies in $\mathcal H$ and $\langle f,k_x\rangle_{\mathcal H}=f(x)$ for every $f\in\mathcal H$. Consequently $\langle k_z,k_x\rangle_{\mathcal H}=k(z,x)=k(x,z)$.

For the canonical construction, let $E_0$ be the real vector space of finitely supported functions $a:X\to\mathbb R$, write $\delta_x$ for the function supported at $x$ with value $1$, and put

$$B(a,b):=\sum_{x\in\operatorname{supp}(a)}\sum_{z\in\operatorname{supp}(b)}a(x)b(z)k(x,z).$$

Let $N:=\{a\in E_0:B(a,a)=0\}$. The canonical space is formed by giving $E_0/N$ its induced inner product and taking a norm completion; the image of $\delta_x$ is denoted $k_x$. For an element $h$ of that completion, its associated function is $x\mapsto\langle h,k_x\rangle$. The quotient, completed inner product, and function identification are justified by the local construction theorem.

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]). A **completion** of $(X,d)$
is a pair $\big((\widehat{X}, \widehat{d}),\, \iota\big)$ in which

- $(\widehat{X}, \widehat{d})$ is a **complete** metric space
  ([[def-complete-metric-space]]);
- $\iota : X \to \widehat{X}$ is an **isometric embedding**, that is
  $\widehat{d}(\iota(x), \iota(y)) = d(x,y)$ for all $x,y \in X$
  ([[def-isometry-and-metric-embedding]]);
- $\iota[X]$ is **dense** in $\widehat{X}$, that is
  $\overline{\iota[X]} = \widehat{X}$
  ([[def-metric-interior-closure-boundary]]).

**The embedding is part of the data, not an afterthought.** A completion is a
pair, and two completions of the same space are compared through their embeddings
([[thm-metric-completion-unique]]); the underlying complete space alone carries
no information about where $X$ sits inside it. This is the same discipline as for
the metric itself: a metric space is a pair, not a set.

**$\iota$ identifies $X$ with a subspace of $\widehat{X}$, metric and topology
included.** An isometric embedding is injective, is an isometry onto its image,
and carries the metric topology of $X$ onto the subspace topology of $\iota[X]$
([[lem-isometry-is-an-embedding]]). So "$X$ is a dense subspace of a complete
space" is an accurate reading of the definition, and the pedantic version with
$\iota$ written out is used only where two completions have to be compared.

**Existence and uniqueness are theorems, not part of the definition.** Under
Countable Choice, every metric space has a completion
([[thm-metric-completion-exists]]) and any two are isometric by a unique
isometry commuting with the embeddings
[[thm-metric-completion-unique]]. Until the first of those is proved, the phrase
*the* completion is not licensed, and it is not used here.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice for assertion 5 and the consequent
existence claim ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space
([[def-metric-space]]) and let $\mathcal{C}$ be the set of all Cauchy sequences
in $X$ ([[def-cauchy-in-metric]]). Then:

1. For all $x = (x_n)$ and $y = (y_n)$ in $\mathcal{C}$ the real sequence
   $\big(d(x_n,y_n)\big)_n$ converges, so
   $$\rho(x,y) \;:=\; \lim_{n} d(x_n,y_n)$$
   is a single well-determined real ([[thm-cauchy-criterion-via-lub]],
   [[lem-limit-unique]]).
2. The relation $x \sim y :\Longleftrightarrow \rho(x,y) = 0$ is an equivalence
   relation on $\mathcal{C}$. Write $\widehat{X} := \mathcal{C}/\!\sim$ for the
   set of its classes and $[x]$ for the class of $x$.
3. $\widehat{d}\big([x],[y]\big) := \rho(x,y)$ does not depend on the chosen
   representatives, and $\widehat{d}$ is a metric on $\widehat{X}$.
4. The map $\iota : X \to \widehat{X}$ sending $p$ to the class of the constant
   sequence at $p$ is an isometric embedding with dense image
   ([[def-isometry-and-metric-embedding]],
   [[def-metric-interior-closure-boundary]]).
5. $(\widehat{X}, \widehat{d})$ is complete.

Consequently $\big((\widehat{X},\widehat{d}), \iota\big)$ is a completion of
$(X,d)$ ([[def-metric-completion]]), and **every metric space has a
completion**.

**The notation is kept honest.** A Cauchy sequence in $X$ need not converge in
$X$, so no symbol $\lim_n x_n$ appears anywhere below; the only limits taken are
limits of *real* sequences, and each is written only after its existence has been
proved. The equivalence relation is defined and verified here rather than cited, as was
done for [[def-integers]], so that the construction is self-contained and its
transitivity argument is visible at the point of use.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $X$ be a
normed space. The published metric completion of the norm metric on $X$ admits
a unique vector-space structure and norm whose induced metric is the
published completion metric and such that the constant sequence embedding
$i:X\to \widehat X$ is a dense linear isometry. With this structure,
$\widehat X$ is a Banach space.

Let $X$ be a normed space. A **completion of $X$** is a pair
$\bigl(\widehat X,\iota\bigr)$ such that

- $\widehat X$ is a Banach space ([[def-banach-space]]);
- $\iota:X\to \widehat X$ is a linear isometry
  ([[def-linear-isometry-and-isometric-isomorphism]]);
- $\iota[X]$ is dense in $\widehat X$
  ([[def-metric-interior-closure-boundary]]).

Equivalently, a completion of a normed space is a completion of its norm metric
([[def-metric-completion]]) together with compatible linear structure on the
complete space.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $X$ be a real or complex inner-product space and let $(\widehat X,\kappa)$ be its norm completion ([[def-completion-of-a-normed-space]]). Then $\widehat X$ carries a unique inner product that extends the given one along $\kappa$ and whose induced length is the completion norm; with it $\widehat X$ is a Hilbert space, and the extension is unique among inner products that extend the given pairing and induce the completion norm.

For vectors $u,v$ in a real or complex inner product space,

$$|\langle u,v\rangle|\le\lVert u\rVert\lVert v\rVert.$$

Equality holds if and only if $u$ and $v$ are linearly dependent, including the case in which either vector is zero.

derivations.claim: Let $E_0$ be the finitely supported functions on $X$ and define $B(a,b)=\sum_{x,z}a(x)b(z)k(x,z)$, where each sum is over the finite supports. Symmetry and bilinearity follow from symmetry of $k$ and finite-sum algebra. For any $a$, listing its finite support gives $B(a,a)\ge0$ by [F1].

For $a,b\in E_0$ and $t\in\mathbb R$, $0\le B(a+tb,a+tb)=B(a,a)+2tB(a,b)+t^2B(b,b)$. If $B(b,b)>0$, nonnegativity of this quadratic for all $t$ gives $B(a,b)^2\le B(a,a)B(b,b)$; if $B(b,b)=0$, its linear coefficient must vanish, so $B(a,b)=0$.

It follows that every $a\in N:=\{a:B(a,a)=0\}$ satisfies $B(a,b)=0$ for every $b\in E_0$. Hence $N$ is a subspace and the form descends to a well-defined positive definite inner product on $Q:=E_0/N$: changing a representative by an element of $N$ does not change any pairing, and a quotient class has zero squared norm exactly when it is the zero class.

The induced inner product makes $Q$ a real inner-product space. By [F2] and [A1], its norm metric has a metric completion with compatible Banach structure, hence a norm completion; the inner product extends uniquely and makes the completion $\widehat Q$ a real Hilbert space.

For each $x\in X$, the image $k_x$ of $[\delta_x]\in Q$ satisfies $\|k_x\|^2=B(\delta_x,\delta_x)=k(x,x)\ge0$. Thus the finite kernel sections are elements of $\widehat Q$, and their span is dense because the image of $Q$ is dense in its completion.

For $a\in E_0$, the quotient pairing gives $\langle[a],k_x\rangle=\sum_{z\in\operatorname{supp}(a)}a(z)k(z,x)$, independently of the representative by [step 3.1]. Given $h\in\widehat Q$, density in [step 4.1] provides an approximating sequence $[a_m]\to h$. By [F3], the real sequence $\langle[a_m],k_x\rangle$ is Cauchy, and if $[b_m]\to h$ is another such sequence then $|\langle[a_m-b_m],k_x\rangle|\le\|[a_m-b_m]\|\|k_x\|\to0$, so its limit is independent of the approximants. The extended inner product also satisfies [F3], hence this limit equals $\langle h,k_x\rangle$.

Define the associated function of $h\in\widehat Q$ by $h(x):=\langle h,k_x\rangle$. Applying the extended pairing to $k_z$ gives $k_z(x)=\langle k_z,k_x\rangle=B(\delta_z,\delta_x)=k(z,x)=k(x,z)$, so $k_x$ is exactly the section $k(\cdot,x)$ and $\langle h,k_x\rangle=h(x)$ for every $h$.

If $h(x)=0$ for every $x\in X$, then $h$ is orthogonal to every section $k_x$ and therefore to their dense span from [step 5.1]. Continuity of the inner product gives $\langle h,h\rangle=0$, so positive definiteness gives $h=0$. Thus the associated-function map is injective and identifies $\widehat Q$ with a Hilbert space of functions having reproducing kernel $k$.

self-adjoint. Then $V$ has an orthonormal basis consisting of eigenvectors of

derivations.claim: Regard $K$ as an endomorphism of $\mathbb R^n$ with its usual dot product. By [A1], $K$ is symmetric, hence self-adjoint. By [F1], there are an orthonormal eigenbasis $q_1,\ldots,q_n$ and real eigenvalues $\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_n$ with $Kq_\ell=\lambda_\ell q_\ell$.
Since $\|q_\ell\|_2=1$, [A1] gives $\lambda_\ell=q_\ell^TKq_\ell\ge0$ for each $\ell$. Thus each $\sqrt{\lambda_\ell}$ is a real number, including when $\lambda_\ell=0$.

For $1\le i\le n$, define $z_i=(\sqrt{\lambda_1}(q_1)_i,\ldots,\sqrt{\lambda_n}(q_n)_i)\in\mathbb R^n$. The spectral decomposition $K=\sum_{\ell=1}^n\lambda_\ell q_\ell q_\ell^T$ then gives $z_i^Tz_j=\sum_{\ell=1}^n\lambda_\ell(q_\ell)_i(q_\ell)_j=K_{ij}=k(x_i,x_j)$ for all $i,j$.

For every $i$, [F1] gives $h(x_i)=\langle h,k_{x_i}\rangle=0$, so $p(x_i)=f(x_i)$. Hence the loss terms in $J(p)$ and $J(f)$ agree.
The norm-contraction clause of [F2] gives $\|p\|_{\mathcal H}\le\|f\|_{\mathcal H}$. Monotonicity of $\Omega$ therefore gives $J(p)\le J(f)$.
Since $f$ is a minimizer, $J(f)\le J(p)$. Thus $J(p)=J(f)$ and $p$ is also a minimizer; by its definition $p$ is a finite linear combination of the sample kernel sections.

Let $X$ be a set, let $\mathcal H$ be a real Hilbert space, and let $\phi:X\to\mathcal H$ be a feature map. Define its kernel by $k(x,z):=\langle\phi(x),\phi(z)\rangle_{\mathcal H}$. For a finite labeled sample $(x_i,y_i)_{i=1}^n$ with $n\ge1$, $x_i\in X$, and $y_i\in\{-1,+1\}$, the **soft-margin support-vector machine** with cost $C>0$ is

$$\min_{w\in\mathcal H,\ b\in\mathbb R,\ \xi\in\mathbb R^n}\ \frac12\|w\|_{\mathcal H}^2+C\sum_{i=1}^n\xi_i$$

subject to

$$y_i\bigl(\langle w,\phi(x_i)\rangle_{\mathcal H}+b\bigr)\ge1-\xi_i,\qquad \xi_i\ge0\quad(1\le i\le n).$$

The bias $b$ is unpenalized. The associated real score is $s_{w,b}(x):=\langle w,\phi(x)\rangle_{\mathcal H}+b$. If a binary label is required, use the deterministic rule $+1$ when $s_{w,b}(x)\ge0$ and $-1$ otherwise. The score is not defined as a probability, and this optimization includes no probability-calibration map.

The **hard-margin** problem removes the slack variables and minimizes $\frac12\|w\|_{\mathcal H}^2$ subject to $y_i(\langle w,\phi(x_i)\rangle_{\mathcal H}+b)\ge1$ for every $i$. In this library, “margin-separable sample” means exactly that this hard-margin feasible set is nonempty; no hard-margin conclusion is asserted for a sample that fails this condition.

Let $n\ge1$ and let $A\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ be nonempty. The following are equivalent.

1. $A$ is compact.
2. $A$ is closed and bounded.
3. $A$ is pseudocompact.
4. Every continuous $f:A\to\mathbb{R}$ attains a maximum and a minimum on $A$.

This theorem is a ZF statement. The nonemptiness hypothesis is necessary for condition 4, because the empty image has neither a maximum nor a minimum.

derivations.claim: The tuple $w=0$, $b=0$, and $\xi_i=1$ is feasible and has objective $Cn$. Every feasible objective is nonnegative, so the primal infimum lies in $[0,Cn]$.

Let $M=\operatorname{span}\{\phi(x_i):1\le i\le n\}$. For any feasible tuple, project $w$ onto $M$ using [F1]. The residual is orthogonal to every $\phi(x_i)$, so all sample scores and constraints are unchanged, while the norm does not increase. Thus minimizing over $M\times\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ has the same infimum as minimizing over the full feature space.

If all labels are $+1$, then $w=0$, $b=1$, and $\xi=0$ is feasible with objective $0$, which is globally minimal by step 1.1. If all labels are $-1$, then $w=0$, $b=-1$, and $\xi=0$ gives the same conclusion.

Suppose both labels occur. Set $R=\max_i\|\phi(x_i)\|$ and let $S$ be the subset of $M\times\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ consisting of feasible tuples with objective at most $Cn$. By step 1.1, $S$ is nonempty. It is closed because the constraints are continuous affine inequalities and the objective is continuous; continuity of each score follows from [F2]. Every tuple in $S$ satisfies $\|w\|\le\sqrt{2Cn}$ and $0\le\xi_i\le n$. Choose indices $i_+$ and $i_-$ with labels $+1$ and $-1$. Their constraints and [F2] give $b\ge1-n-\sqrt{2Cn}R$ and $b\le n-1+\sqrt{2Cn}R$, so $b$ is bounded. By [F3], an orthonormal basis identifies the finite-dimensional product space with $\mathbb R^d$ for some $d\ge1$; hence $S$ is a nonempty closed bounded subset of that Euclidean space. By [F4], the continuous objective attains a minimum on $S$. Any feasible tuple outside $S$ has objective greater than $Cn$, whereas $S$ contains a feasible tuple of objective $Cn$; therefore this minimum is also the global primal minimum. By step 1.2 it is a full-space minimizer with $w\in M$.

citations.quote: Let $n\ge1$, let $C>0$, and let $(x_i,y_i)_{i=1}^n$ be a finite labeled sample with $y_i\in\{-1,+1\}$ in a real Hilbert feature space $\mathcal H$, with feature map $\phi$. The soft-margin SVM primal has a finite attained minimum. At least one minimizing tuple has its weight vector in $M:=\operatorname{span}\{\phi(x_i):1\le i\le n\}$. This conclusion includes samples with only one label and does not assert uniqueness of the bias or slack variables.

Let $E$ be a real inner-product space, let $M\subseteq E$ be a finite-dimensional subspace, and let $f\in E$. There is a unique $p\in M$ such that $f-p$ is orthogonal to every vector of $M$. This vector is the unique nearest point in $M$ to $f$, and it satisfies $\|p\|\le\|f\|$. The conclusion does not require $E$ to be complete.

Let $k$ be a real positive semidefinite kernel on a set $X$, let $n\ge1$, and let $x_1,\ldots,x_n\in X$. There are vectors $z_1,\ldots,z_n\in\mathbb R^n$ such that $k(x_i,x_j)=z_i^Tz_j$ for every $1\le i,j\le n$. The vectors may be zero and need not be linearly independent.

A subset is convex when it contains the segment joining each pair of its
points ([[def-convex-subset-of-euclidean-space]]). A function
$F:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ is proper if it never equals
$-\infty$ and is finite at at least one point. Its domain is
$\operatorname{dom}F=\{x:F(x)<+\infty\}$. Its epigraph is
$\operatorname{epi}F=\{(x,t):F(x)\le t\}$. It is closed convex when its
epigraph is a closed convex set. For a nonempty convex set $S$,
$\operatorname{aff}S$ is its smallest containing affine subspace and
$\operatorname{ri}S$ is its interior relative to $\operatorname{aff}S$.

Let $n\ge1$, let $m,p\in\mathbb N$ with zero allowed, let
$f_0,g_1,\ldots,g_m$ be proper closed convex functions on $\mathbb R^n$,
let $A\in\mathbb R^{p\times n}$ have full row rank, and let
$b\in\mathbb R^p$. Full row rank means that the rows are linearly
independent, vacuously when $p=0$. The common domain is
$D=\operatorname{dom}f_0\cap\bigcap_{i=1}^m\operatorname{dom}g_i$. The primal
problem is to minimize $f_0(x)$ over $x\in D$ satisfying $Ax=b$ and
$g_i(x)\le0$. An inequality is removable if, with
$D_{-i}=\operatorname{dom}f_0\cap\bigcap_{j\ne i}\operatorname{dom}g_j$,
$D_{-i}\subseteq\operatorname{dom}g_i$ and $g_i(x)\le0$ for every $x\in D_{-i}$.
Then $D=D_{-i}$, so removing that function and its inequality leaves the
feasible set unchanged. While a removable inequality exists, delete the one
with smallest original index, recomputing $D_{-i}$ using the currently retained
family after each deletion. Stop when none is removable, then relabel the
remaining inequalities consecutively in their original order and let $m$
denote their number. An inequality that is nonpositive only on $D$
but whose function domain restricts $D$ is not removable. Unless stated
otherwise, the inequalities below are the remaining ones after only these
domain-preserving deletions. The primal value is
$$
p^*=\inf\{f_0(x):x\in D,\ Ax=b,\ g_i(x)\le0\text{ for all }i\}.
$$

For $\lambda\in\mathbb R^m_+$ and $\nu\in\mathbb R^p$, the extended
Lagrangian is
$$
L(x,\lambda,\nu)=\begin{cases}f_0(x)+\lambda^Tg(x)+\nu^T(Ax-b),&x\in D,\\+\infty,&x\notin D.\end{cases}
$$
The dual function and dual value are
$$
q(\lambda,\nu)=\inf_{x\in\mathbb R^n}L(x,\lambda,\nu),\qquad d^*=\sup_{\lambda\ge0,\ \nu\in\mathbb R^p}q(\lambda,\nu).
$$
The dual supremum is attained when some admissible $(\lambda,\nu)$ has
$q(\lambda,\nu)=d^*$; the optimal duality gap is $p^*-d^*$ when both values
are finite.

Slater's condition means that there is
$x_s\in\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}f_0)\cap
\bigcap_i\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}g_i)$ with $Ax_s=b$ and
$g_i(x_s)<0$ for every remaining inequality. Relative interior is used in
the affine hull of each domain, so the domain need not have ambient interior.

Consider the finite-dimensional convex program of
[[def-convex-program-duality-and-slater-condition]]. Assume its equality
matrix has independent rows, Slater's condition holds, and the finite primal
value $p^*\in\mathbb R$ is attained at $x_*$. Then there are
$\lambda_*\ge0$ and $\nu_*$ such that
$$q(\lambda_*,\nu_*)=d^*=p^*.$$
Moreover, every inequality multiplier satisfies
$\lambda_{*,i}g_i(x_*)=0$. The Slater and attainment hypotheses do not assert
that a primal minimizer is unique.

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R$
be $C^2$. Let $p,m\in\mathbb N$ with zero allowed; when the target
dimension is positive, let $h:U\to\mathbb R^p$ and
$g=(g_1,\ldots,g_m):U\to\mathbb R^m$ be componentwise $C^2$, and when it
is zero use the unique empty map. The $C^2$ convention for positive
dimensions is [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]].
The $C^2$ inequality program is to minimize $f(x)$ subject to
$h(x)=0$ and $g_i(x)\le0$ for every $i$. Its feasible set is
$C=\{x\in U:h(x)=0,\ g_i(x)\le0\ (1\le i\le m)\}$. A feasible point $x_*$ is
a local minimizer if some open neighborhood $V$ of $x_*$ satisfies
$f(x_*)\le f(y)$ for every $y\in C\cap V$.

At a feasible $x$, the active set is
$I(x)=\{i:g_i(x)=0\}$. The Bouligand tangent cone and linearized cone are,
respectively,
$$
T_C(x)=\{d:\exists\,t_k>0,\ t_k\downarrow0,\ d_k\to d,\ x+t_kd_k\in C\},
$$
and
$$
\mathcal L_C(x)=\{d:Dh(x)d=0,\ Dg_i(x)d\le0\text{ for every }i\in I(x)\}.
$$
Gradients are column vectors and $Dg_i(x)d=\nabla g_i(x)^Td$.

The linear independence constraint qualification (LICQ) holds at $x$ when the rows of $Dh(x)$ together with
$\{\nabla g_i(x)^T:i\in I(x)\}$ are linearly independent. MFCQ holds at $x$
when $Dh(x)$ has full row rank (its rows are linearly independent) and there is $w\in\ker Dh(x)$ with
$Dg_i(x)w<0$ for every active $i$; the latter condition is vacuous if
$I(x)=\varnothing$. Here full row rank for a matrix with zero rows is
understood vacuously.

The Mangasarian–Fromovitz constraint qualification (MFCQ) is the condition
just stated. The Karush–Kuhn–Tucker (KKT) system is the stationarity,
feasibility, dual-feasibility, and complementarity system below.

For $\nu\in\mathbb R^p$ and $\lambda\in\mathbb R^m$, the Lagrangian and KKT
system are
$$
L(x,\nu,\lambda)=f(x)+\nu^Th(x)+\lambda^Tg(x),
$$
$$
h(x)=0,\quad g(x)\le0,\quad \lambda\ge0,\quad \lambda_i g_i(x)=0\ (1\le i\le m),\quad \nabla_xL(x,\nu,\lambda)=0.
$$
The critical cone for a KKT tuple is
$\mathcal K(x,\nu,\lambda)=\mathcal L_C(x)\cap
\{d:\nabla f(x)^Td=0\}$. These definitions use the differentiability and
gradient conventions of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]],
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]], and [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]].

Let $m\ge0$ be an integer. Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and convex,
and suppose the objective $f:U\to\mathbb R$ and inequalities
$g_i:U\to\mathbb R$ $(1\le i\le m)$ are differentiable and convex.
Let the equalities be $Ax=b$ and define the feasible set
$C=\{x\in U:Ax=b,\ g_i(x)\le0\ (1\le i\le m)\}$. If a feasible tuple
$(x_*,\nu,\lambda)$ satisfies the KKT conditions with $\lambda\ge0$, then
$x_*$ is a global minimizer over the feasible set $C$. Moreover,
$-\nabla f(x_*)\in N_C(x_*)$, where the normal cone has the convention of
[[def-kkt-residual-and-normal-cone]].

derivations.claim: Let $(w_*,b_*,\xi_*)$ be any primal minimizer, which exists by [F1], and let $M=\operatorname{span}\{\phi(x_i):1\le i\le n\}$. Project $w_*$ onto $M$ using [F2]; its residual is orthogonal to every $\phi(x_i)$, so the projection preserves all margins and slacks. If the residual were nonzero, [F3] would give a strictly smaller squared norm and hence a strictly smaller objective, contradicting minimality because the regularization coefficient is $1/2>0$. Thus every primal minimizer has $w_*\in M$.

Identify $M$ with a Euclidean space using an orthonormal basis. In the finite-dimensional variable space $M\times\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$, the objective is a proper continuous convex function and the $2n$ inequality constraints are continuous affine functions with the sign convention [F7]. No inequality is removed by the domain-preserving convention in [F5]: all functions have full domain, and sending the corresponding $\xi_i\to-\infty$ makes either constraint function positive. There are no primal equality rows, so the full-row-rank condition in [F5] holds vacuously.

The point $w=0$, $b=0$, $\xi_i=2$ has strict slack in every constraint: $1-\xi_i-y_i(\langle w,\phi(x_i)\rangle+b)=-1<0$ and $-\xi_i=-2<0$. The objective and all constraint domains are the whole finite-dimensional variable space, so this point lies in their relative interiors. Together with the finite attained primal value from [F1], this verifies every hypothesis of [F6].

Write the margin constraints as $g_i^{(m)}:=1-\xi_i-y_i(\langle w,\phi(x_i)\rangle+b)\le0$ and the nonnegative-slack constraints as $g_i^{(s)}:=-\xi_i\le0$. Give them multipliers $\alpha_i\ge0$ and $\mu_i\ge0$, respectively. The Lagrangian is $L=\frac12\|w\|^2+C\sum_i\xi_i+\sum_i\alpha_i g_i^{(m)}+\sum_i\mu_i g_i^{(s)}$.

Put $v:=\sum_i\alpha_i y_i\phi(x_i)$. The terms of $L$ depending on $w$ are $\frac12\|w\|^2-\langle w,v\rangle=\frac12\|w-v\|^2-\frac12\|v\|^2$, so their infimum is $-\frac12\|v\|^2$. The infimum over the unrestricted bias $b$ is finite exactly when $\sum_i\alpha_i y_i=0$, and the infimum over each unrestricted $\xi_i$ is finite exactly when $C-\alpha_i-\mu_i=0$. Thus the dual-feasible conditions are $\sum_i\alpha_i y_i=0$ and $0\le\alpha_i\le C$.

Apply [F6] using the verified hypotheses in [step 3.1]. It gives an attained dual optimum $(\alpha,\mu)$ with the same value as the primal optimum and complementarity for both families $g_i^{(m)}$ and $g_i^{(s)}$. At any fixed primal minimizer, these equal values and complementarity make $L$ attain its unconstrained infimum; its derivatives in $w$, $b$, and each $\xi_i$ therefore vanish.

For any finite list $u_1,\ldots,u_m\in X$ and $c_1,\ldots,c_m\in\mathbb R$, symmetry and bilinearity of the real inner product give $\sum_{r,s}c_rc_sk(u_r,u_s)=\langle\sum_r c_r\phi(u_r),\sum_s c_s\phi(u_s)\rangle=\|\sum_r c_r\phi(u_r)\|^2\ge0$. Thus the feature-induced kernel $k$ is real positive semidefinite, so its sample Gram matrix satisfies the hypothesis of [F4]. Since $k(x_i,x_j)=\langle\phi(x_i),\phi(x_j)\rangle$, $\|v\|^2=\sum_{i,j}\alpha_i\alpha_jy_iy_jk(x_i,x_j)$. By [F4], the matrix $(y_iy_jk(x_i,x_j))_{i,j}$ is the Gram matrix of $y_i z_i$, so its quadratic form is nonnegative. Hence the displayed dual objective is concave. Its equality row has coefficient vector $y\ne0$, because $n\ge1$ and each $y_i\in\{-1,+1\}$, so that row is independent.

Differentiating the Lagrangian of [step 3.2] gives $w=\sum_i\alpha_i y_i\phi(x_i)$, $\sum_i\alpha_i y_i=0$, and $C-\alpha_i-\mu_i=0$. The last equation and $\mu_i\ge0$ give $\alpha_i\le C$; together with $\alpha_i\ge0$ these are the dual box constraints. The complementarity equations supplied by [F6] are $\alpha_i g_i^{(m)}=0$ and $\mu_i g_i^{(s)}=0$, which are exactly the two equations in the Statement.

The finite-dimensional primal has differentiable convex objective and affine convex constraints on the open convex variable space identified in [step 2.1]. Thus [F8] certifies that any feasible tuple satisfying the stationarity and complementarity equations is a global primal minimizer. If $0<\alpha_i<C$, then $\mu_i=C-\alpha_i>0$, so $\mu_i\xi_i=0$ forces $\xi_i=0$; then $\alpha_i g_i^{(m)}=0$ forces the signed margin to equal $1$. Finally, for any input $x$, stationarity gives the score $s(x)=\sum_i\alpha_i y_i k(x_i,x)+b$.

A **real kernel** on a set $X$ is a function $k:X\times X\to\mathbb R$. It is **positive semidefinite** if it is symmetric and, for every integer $n\ge1$, every $x_1,\ldots,x_n\in X$, and every $c_1,\ldots,c_n\in\mathbb R$,

$$\sum_{i=1}^n\sum_{j=1}^n c_i c_j k(x_i,x_j)\ge0.$$

A **real reproducing kernel Hilbert space with kernel $k$** is a real Hilbert space $\mathcal H$ of functions $X\to\mathbb R$ such that, for each $x\in X$, the section $k_x:=k(\cdot,x)$ lies in $\mathcal H$ and $\langle f,k_x\rangle_{\mathcal H}=f(x)$ for every $f\in\mathcal H$. Consequently $\langle k_z,k_x\rangle_{\mathcal H}=k(z,x)=k(x,z)$.

For the canonical construction, let $E_0$ be the real vector space of finitely supported functions $a:X\to\mathbb R$, write $\delta_x$ for the function supported at $x$ with value $1$, and put

$$B(a,b):=\sum_{x\in\operatorname{supp}(a)}\sum_{z\in\operatorname{supp}(b)}a(x)b(z)k(x,z).$$

Let $N:=\{a\in E_0:B(a,a)=0\}$. The canonical space is formed by giving $E_0/N$ its induced inner product and taking a norm completion; the image of $\delta_x$ is denoted $k_x$. For an element $h$ of that completion, its associated function is $x\mapsto\langle h,k_x\rangle$. The quotient, completed inner product, and function identification are justified by the local construction theorem.

derivations.claim: For any finite sample $x_1,\ldots,x_m\in\mathbb R^p$ and coefficients $c_1,\ldots,c_m\in\mathbb R$, the linear Gram quadratic form is $\sum_{i,j}c_ic_jx_i^Tx_j=\|\sum_i c_ix_i\|_2^2\ge0$. Thus $k_{\rm lin}$ satisfies the nonnegative-form condition in [F1], and it is symmetric because $x^Tz=z^Tx$.

For $\alpha=(\alpha_0,\ldots,\alpha_p)\in\mathbb N_0^{p+1}$ with $|\alpha|=d$, define $\psi_\alpha(x)=\sqrt{d!/\alpha_0!\cdots\alpha_p!}\prod_{r=1}^p x_r^{\alpha_r}$. The multinomial theorem gives $(1+x^Tz)^d=\sum_{|\alpha|=d}\psi_\alpha(x)\psi_\alpha(z)$.

Therefore, for every finite sample and coefficients, $\sum_{i,j}c_ic_jk_d(x_i,x_j)=\sum_{|\alpha|=d}(\sum_i c_i\psi_\alpha(x_i))^2\ge0$. The polynomial kernel is symmetric and positive semidefinite by [F1].
When $p=2$ and $d=2$, the six multi-indices in [step 1.2] give $h(x)=(1,\sqrt2x_1,\sqrt2x_2,x_1^2,x_2^2,\sqrt2x_1x_2)$, so the stated feature identity holds.

A **real reproducing kernel Hilbert space with kernel $k$** is a real Hilbert space $\mathcal H$ of functions $X\to\mathbb R$ such that, for each $x\in X$, the section $k_x:=k(\cdot,x)$ lies in $\mathcal H$ and $\langle f,k_x\rangle_{\mathcal H}=f(x)$ for every $f\in\mathcal H$. Let $N:=\{a\in E_0:B(a,a)=0\}$. The canonical space is formed by giving $E_0/N$ its induced inner product and taking a norm completion; the image of $\delta_x$ is denoted $k_x$. derivations.claim: For each sample point put $a_i=c_i\exp(-\|x_i\|_2^2/(2\sigma^2))$. The identity $\|x_i-x_j\|_2^2=\|x_i\|_2^2+\|x_j\|_2^2-2x_i^Tx_j$ gives $\sum_{i,j}c_ic_jk_\sigma(x_i,x_j)=\sum_{i,j}a_i a_j\exp(x_i^Tx_j/\sigma^2)$.

For each fixed pair $i,j$, the exponential series has the absolutely convergent multi-index expansion $\exp(x_i^Tx_j/\sigma^2)=\sum_{\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^p}(x_i^\alpha x_j^\alpha)/(\sigma^{2|\alpha|}\alpha!)$, since the corresponding series of absolute values is $\prod_{r=1}^p\exp(|x_{ir}x_{jr}|/\sigma^2)<\infty$. The sample sums are finite, so they can be interchanged with this absolutely convergent series.

Substitution into [step 1.1] yields $\sum_{i,j}c_ic_jk_\sigma(x_i,x_j)=\sum_{\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^p}\frac{1}{\sigma^{2|\alpha|}\alpha!}(\sum_i a_ix_i^\alpha)^2\ge0$. Symmetry of $k_\sigma$ is immediate from $\|x-z\|_2=\|z-x\|_2$, so [F1] proves positive semidefiniteness; zero eigenvalues or repeated points do not affect the sum-of-squares argument.

citations.quote:
Let $X$ be a set, let $\mathcal H$ be a real Hilbert space, and let $\phi:X\to\mathcal H$ be a feature map. Define its kernel by $k(x,z):=\langle\phi(x),\phi(z)\rangle_{\mathcal H}$. For a finite labeled sample $(x_i,y_i)_{i=1}^n$ with $n\ge1$, $x_i\in X$, and $y_i\in\{-1,+1\}$, the **soft-margin support-vector machine** with cost $C>0$ is

$$\min_{w\in\mathcal H,\ b\in\mathbb R,\ \xi\in\mathbb R^n}\ \frac12\|w\|_{\mathcal H}^2+C\sum_{i=1}^n\xi_i$$

subject to

$$y_i\bigl(\langle w,\phi(x_i)\rangle_{\mathcal H}+b\bigr)\ge1-\xi_i,\qquad \xi_i\ge0\quad(1\le i\le n).$$

The bias $b$ is unpenalized. The associated real score is $s_{w,b}(x):=\langle w,\phi(x)\rangle_{\mathcal H}+b$. If a binary label is required, use the deterministic rule $+1$ when $s_{w,b}(x)\ge0$ and $-1$ otherwise. The score is not defined as a probability, and this optimization includes no probability-calibration map.

The **hard-margin** problem removes the slack variables and minimizes $\frac12\|w\|_{\mathcal H}^2$ subject to $y_i(\langle w,\phi(x_i)\rangle_{\mathcal H}+b)\ge1$ for every $i$. In this library, “margin-separable sample” means exactly that this hard-margin feasible set is nonempty; no hard-margin conclusion is asserted for a sample that fails this condition.

For $x,z\in\mathbb R^p$ with $p\ge1$, the linear kernel $k_{\rm lin}(x,z)=x^Tz$ and, for each integer $d\ge0$, the inhomogeneous polynomial kernel $k_d(x,z)=(1+x^Tz)^d$ are positive semidefinite. When $p=2$ and $d=2$, the polynomial kernel has the explicit feature map $h(x)=(1,\sqrt2x_1,\sqrt2x_2,x_1^2,x_2^2,\sqrt2x_1x_2)$ with $k_2(x,z)=h(x)^Th(z)$.

Hence every feasible objective satisfies $\frac12w^2\ge\frac12$. The candidate $w=1,b=0$ satisfies both constraints with equality and has objective $1/2$, so it attains the minimum.

citations.quote:
Let $X$ be a set, let $\mathcal H$ be a real Hilbert space, and let $\phi:X\to\mathcal H$ be a feature map. Define its kernel by $k(x,z):=\langle\phi(x),\phi(z)\rangle_{\mathcal H}$. For a finite labeled sample $(x_i,y_i)_{i=1}^n$ with $n\ge1$, $x_i\in X$, and $y_i\in\{-1,+1\}$, the **soft-margin support-vector machine** with cost $C>0$ is

$$\min_{w\in\mathcal H,\ b\in\mathbb R,\ \xi\in\mathbb R^n}\ \frac12\|w\|_{\mathcal H}^2+C\sum_{i=1}^n\xi_i$$

subject to

$$y_i\bigl(\langle w,\phi(x_i)\rangle_{\mathcal H}+b\bigr)\ge1-\xi_i,\qquad \xi_i\ge0\quad(1\le i\le n).$$

The bias $b$ is unpenalized. The associated real score is $s_{w,b}(x):=\langle w,\phi(x)\rangle_{\mathcal H}+b$. If a binary label is required, use the deterministic rule $+1$ when $s_{w,b}(x)\ge0$ and $-1$ otherwise. The score is not defined as a probability, and this optimization includes no probability-calibration map.

The **hard-margin** problem removes the slack variables and minimizes $\frac12\|w\|_{\mathcal H}^2$ subject to $y_i(\langle w,\phi(x_i)\rangle_{\mathcal H}+b)\ge1$ for every $i$. In this library, “margin-separable sample” means exactly that this hard-margin feasible set is nonempty; no hard-margin conclusion is asserted for a sample that fails this condition.

Let $n\ge1$, $C>0$, let $\mathcal H$ be a real Hilbert space, and let $\phi:X\to\mathcal H$ be a feature map with kernel $k(x,z)=\langle\phi(x),\phi(z)\rangle_{\mathcal H}$. For any finite sample $(x_i,y_i)_{i=1}^n$ with $y_i\in\{-1,+1\}$, the soft-margin SVM primal attains its minimum. Its Lagrangian dual is

$$\max_{\alpha\in\mathbb R^n}\ \sum_{i=1}^n\alpha_i-\frac12\sum_{i=1}^n\sum_{j=1}^n\alpha_i\alpha_jy_iy_jk(x_i,x_j)$$

subject to $0\le\alpha_i\le C$ for every $i$ and $\sum_i\alpha_i y_i=0$. The dual maximum is attained and equals the primal minimum. For every primal minimizer there are dual multipliers $\alpha_i$ and $\mu_i$ such that

$$w=\sum_{i=1}^n\alpha_i y_i\phi(x_i),\qquad \sum_{i=1}^n\alpha_i y_i=0,\qquad C-\alpha_i-\mu_i=0,$$

$$\alpha_i\bigl(1-\xi_i-y_i(\langle w,\phi(x_i)\rangle+b)\bigr)=0,\qquad \mu_i\xi_i=0,$$

with $\alpha_i\ge0$ and $\mu_i\ge0$. Conversely, any primal-feasible tuple and nonnegative multipliers satisfying these stationarity and complementarity equations are globally optimal. An index with $\alpha_i>0$ is a support vector; if $0<\alpha_i<C$, then $\xi_i=0$ and its signed margin equals $1$. The single dual equality row is independent because $(y_1,\ldots,y_n)\ne0$.

For $x,z\in\mathbb R^p$ with $p\ge1$, the linear kernel $k_{\rm lin}(x,z)=x^Tz$ and, for each integer $d\ge0$, the inhomogeneous polynomial kernel $k_d(x,z)=(1+x^Tz)^d$ are positive semidefinite. When $p=2$ and $d=2$, the polynomial kernel has the explicit feature map $h(x)=(1,\sqrt2x_1,\sqrt2x_2,x_1^2,x_2^2,\sqrt2x_1x_2)$ with $k_2(x,z)=h(x)^Th(z)$.

derivations.claim: The feature map in [F3] realizes the stated linear kernel. At $w=0$, $b=-1$, the scores at all three observations equal $-1$. Their signed margins are respectively $1,-1,1$, so $\xi=(0,2,0)$ satisfies every soft-margin constraint, with objective $2C$.

For any feasible tuple, let $t=w+b$, the score at $x=1$. The two observations at $x=1$ require $\xi_2\ge\max(0,1-t)$ and $\xi_3\ge\max(0,1+t)$. If $-1\le t\le1$ these lower bounds sum to $2$; if $t>1$, the second is $1+t>2$; and if $t<-1$, the first is $1-t>2$. Thus $\xi_2+\xi_3\ge2$ for every feasible tuple, and its objective is at least $C(\xi_2+\xi_3)\ge2C$.

The candidate in [step 1.1] is therefore globally optimal. For $\alpha=(0,C,C)$ and $\mu=(C,0,0)$, $\sum_i\alpha_i y_i\phi(x_i)=C-C=0=w$, $\sum_i\alpha_i y_i=C-C=0$, and $C-\alpha_i-\mu_i=0$ for all three indices. Each margin constraint is active, so $\alpha_i g_i^{(m)}=0$; also $\mu_i\xi_i=0$ for each $i$. These are the KKT conditions in [F2].

The dual objective is $\sum_i\alpha_i-\frac12\|\sum_i\alpha_i y_i\phi(x_i)\|^2=2C$, equal to the primal value. The score at $x=1$ is $-1$, while the empirical positive-label frequency among the two observations at $x=1$ is $1/2$. The logistic transform of the score is $(1+e)^{-1}\ne1/2$; the SVM optimization does not assert that this transformed value is a probability.
